topics.summary: Two subordinating conjunctions that send the verb to the end.

explanation.heading: The verb goes last
explanation.text: weil and dass introduce a subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb moves to the very end: … weil er dort keine Sprachprobleme hat.

explanation.heading: weil answers Warum?
explanation.text: Dependent clauses with weil explain the reason. They answer why questions: Warum?

explanation.heading: dass after verbs of thinking and saying
explanation.text: Verbs such as hoffen, glauben, wissen often go before dependent clauses with dass.

explanation.heading: Spoken German
explanation.text: When speaking colloquially it is possible to link two main clauses with weil, with a pause instead of the moved verb — the document prints the example with dots to mark it.

rules: weil and dass send the conjugated verb to the end of the clause.
weil gives the reason and answers Warum?
dass follows verbs like hoffen, glauben, wissen, finden.
A comma separates the main clause from the subordinate clause.
The colloquial weil + main-clause order exists in speech but is not the written standard.

examples.note: hat at the end

examples.de: Ich möchte im Ausland studieren, weil Auslandserfahrung wichtig ist.
examples.note: ist at the end

examples.de: Wir finden, dass Köln eine schöne Stadt ist.
examples.note: dass after finden

topics.summary: The same reason stated the other way round, with the consequence as a main clause.

explanation.heading: Reason first, consequence second
explanation.text: A weil clause names the reason; darum, deshalb, deswegen and daher turn the sentence round so that the reason comes first as a main clause and the consequence follows.

explanation.heading: Position 1
explanation.text: The connector fills position 1 of the second main clause, so the conjugated verb comes second and the subject third: … darum gehe ich jeden zweiten Tag walken.

explanation.heading: Four words, one meaning
explanation.text: The document lists darum, deshalb and deswegen as interchangeable in both examples, with daher in the heading.

rules: darum, deshalb, deswegen, daher introduce the consequence, not the reason.
They occupy position 1, so the verb comes second and the subject follows it.
Weil ich Sport machen soll, … becomes Ich soll Sport machen, darum …
The clause they open is a main clause, so the verb does not move to the end.

topics.summary: An if-clause that can stand after or before the main clause.

explanation.heading: Two orders
explanation.text: The document prints the same content twice: Hauptsatz + Nebensatz (Rui bekommt Zinsen, wenn …) and Nebensatz + Hauptsatz (Wenn Rui Geld anlegen will, kann er …).

explanation.heading: The verb still goes last in the wenn clause
explanation.text: wenn is a subordinating conjunction, so its clause always ends with the conjugated verb — hat, macht, will, macht.

explanation.heading: When the wenn clause comes first
explanation.text: The whole subordinate clause counts as position 1, so the main clause begins with its verb: …, kann er es auf ein Sparkonto einzahlen; …, kostet die EC-Karte 6,50 € pro Jahr.

rules: wenn introduces the condition and sends its verb to the end.
The wenn clause may follow or precede the main clause.
A leading wenn clause fills position 1, so the main clause starts with the conjugated verb.
A comma always separates the two clauses.

topics.titleEn: als — a single point in the past
topics.summary: The temporal conjunction for something that happened once.

explanation.heading: What als does
explanation.text: als names a point of time in the past — one occasion, not a repeated one.

explanation.heading: The verb goes last
explanation.text: als introduces a subordinate clause: … als der Krimiautor eintraf; … als er an der Kasse zahlen wollte.

explanation.heading: Either order
explanation.text: The document shows both arrangements of the same two sentences, with the als clause after and before the main clause. When it comes first, the main clause opens with its verb: Als der Krimiautor eintraf, gab es ein großes Gedränge.

rules: als names a single point of time in the past.
The conjugated verb goes to the end of the als clause.
The als clause may stand before or after the main clause.
A leading als clause is position 1, so the main clause begins with the verb.

examples.de: Es gab ein großes Gedränge, als der Krimiautor eintraf.
examples.note: main clause first

examples.de: Ruis Portemonnaie war weg, als er an der Kasse zahlen wollte.
examples.note: the modal wollte closes the clause

topics.summary: seit(dem) marks a starting point that still holds; bis marks an end point.

explanation.heading: seit(dem)
explanation.text: The clause names the moment something started, and the situation has lasted since: Beate hat dauernd Schmerzen, seit(dem) sie an ihrer Masterarbeit arbeitet. The document marks this with the symbol • →.

explanation.heading: bis
explanation.text: The clause names the moment something will stop or stopped: Es dauert noch 2 Wochen, bis Beate zu Dr. Rosmann gehen kann. The document marks it • → •, an interval with both ends.

explanation.heading: Both orders
explanation.text: Each conjunction is shown after and before the main clause. A leading subordinate clause is position 1, so the main clause begins with its verb: Seit(dem) Beate so viel arbeitet, hat sie dauernd Schmerzen.

explanation.heading: Tenses
explanation.text: The examples pair present with present (arbeitet – hat) and past with past (bekam – dauerte).

rules: seit(dem) names the starting point of a situation that still holds.
bis names the end point of a period.
Both are subordinating conjunctions: the verb goes to the end.
Either clause can come first; a leading subordinate clause fills position 1.
seitdem and seit are both possible in this use.

examples.de: Beate hat dauernd Schmerzen, seit(dem) sie an ihrer Masterarbeit arbeitet.
examples.note: seit(dem) — the starting point

examples.note: subordinate clause first

examples.note: subordinate clause first

topics.summary: ob for yes/no questions, the question word otherwise — and the verb at the end.

explanation.heading: Yes/no questions take ob
explanation.text: If the direct question is a yes/no question, the indirect question begins with ob: Gibt es auch Führungen …? → Ich möchte wissen, ob es auch Führungen … gibt.

explanation.heading: W-questions keep their word
explanation.text: If the direct question begins with a question word, the indirect question will begin with the same question word: wie lange, wo, welches.

explanation.heading: The verb moves to the end
explanation.text: In every example the conjugated verb closes the clause: gibt, dauert, ist, ist.

explanation.heading: Why use it
explanation.text: The introductory phrases — Ich möchte wissen, Können Sie mir sagen, Können Sie mir zeigen — make the question more polite.

rules: Yes/no question → ob.
W-question → the same question word.
The conjugated verb goes to the end of the indirect question.
The introduction is a main clause and keeps its own word order.
A comma separates the introduction from the indirect question.

topics.summary: Gender and number come from the noun; the case comes from the relative clause.

explanation.heading: The forms
explanation.text: The table is almost the definite article: Nom. der, das, die, die; Akk. den, das, die, die; Dat. dem, dem, der, denen. Only the dative plural denen differs.

explanation.heading: Where gender comes from
explanation.text: The gender (der, die, das) and whether the pronoun is singular or plural depends on the noun which the relative pronoun is referring to: Ich hatte einen Berater, der sehr kompetent war.

explanation.heading: Where case comes from
explanation.text: The case depends either on the verb in the relative clause (treffen + accusative) or on the preposition (hören von + dative) — not on the main clause.

explanation.heading: Position
explanation.text: Relative clauses are dependent clauses, so the verb goes to the end, and the clause often begins directly after the word it is referring to.

rules: Gender and number come from the noun in the main clause.
Case comes from the verb or the preposition inside the relative clause.
The forms match the definite article except in the dative plural: denen.
The conjugated verb stands at the end of the relative clause.
The relative clause often follows its noun immediately.

examples.de: Ich hatte einen Berater, der sehr kompetent war.
examples.note: der Berater is masculine; the pronoun is the subject of the relative clause, so nominative

examples.de: Nom. der das die die

examples.de: Akk. den den die die
examples.note: the accusative row as printed in the document

topics.summary: was refers to a whole sentence or to a pronoun, never to an ordinary noun.

explanation.heading: Two uses
explanation.text: The document lists exactly two: was refers to a previous sentence, or to a pronoun.

explanation.heading: To a previous sentence
explanation.text: Wir duzen unsere Professoren, was komplett anders ist — was stands for the whole statement before the comma.

explanation.heading: To a pronoun
explanation.text: Ich mag alles, was mit Sport zu tun hat — was picks up alles. The same applies to das, nichts, etwas, vieles.

explanation.heading: Word order
explanation.text: It is a relative clause like any other: the conjugated verb closes it — ist, hat.

rules: was refers to a previous sentence or to a pronoun.
An ordinary noun takes der, das or die instead.
The verb goes to the end of the was clause.
A comma introduces the clause.

examples.de: Wir duzen unsere Professoren, was komplett anders ist.
examples.note: was refers to the whole preceding statement

examples.de: Ich mag alles, was mit Sport zu tun hat.
examples.note: was refers to the pronoun alles
